lines.text: Desert rock art, Berber kings, Roman towns, Ottoman corsairs and a hard-won freedom. This is the story of Algeria, Africa's largest country.
Most of Algeria lies in the Sahara, a desert that has turned green and dry again many times, with lakes and herders only six thousand years ago.
On the plateau of Tassili n'Ajjer, people painted thousands of scenes on the rocks, from a time when the desert was green.
In the north, the Berber kingdom of Numidia rose under Massinissa, first an ally of Rome, and later, under Jugurtha, its enemy.
Rome took the land, and in the Aures mountains built Timgad, a colony laid out on a perfect grid.
At Hippo on the coast, Bishop Augustine wrote his Confessions and the City of God, shaping Western Christianity for centuries.
Around 944, Algiers was founded on the Mediterranean, the white city that is now the capital.
In the sixteenth century Algiers came under the Ottomans, and its Barbary corsairs raided ships across the sea.
Emir Abdelkader, born in 1808, would lead the resistance when France invaded.
In 1830 France landed at Algiers. The conquest of the whole country would take decades.
Albert Camus was born in Algeria in 1913, and wrote The Stranger under its sun. He won the Nobel Prize in 1957.
Ahmed Ben Bella, born in 1916, would lead the fight for independence and become the first president.
In Oran, rai music was born, Bedouin songs mixed with modern sounds, later carried around the world by Khaled.
Houari Boumediene was born in 1932. He would seize power in 1965 and take the oil and gas into national hands.
Abdelaziz Bouteflika, born in 1937, would one day hold the presidency for twenty years.
And Abdelmadjid Tebboune, born in 1945, is president today.
In 1954 the National Liberation Front was founded to win independence by force.
The war against France began that same year, fought in Algeria and in France itself, at a terrible cost to civilians.
In 1957 the French army set out to break the FLN in the Casbah of Algiers, and became notorious for its use of torture.
In March 1962, after years of bloodshed, France and the FLN signed the Evian Accords and the war was over.
That summer, after eight years of war and more than a century of French rule, Algeria was independent.
Zinedine Zidane, born in France to Algerian parents, led France to the World Cup in 1998, and later won the Champions League as a manager.
In the 1990s, Algeria was torn again, by a civil war between the army and Islamist groups that lasted a decade.
In 2019 millions marched peacefully in the Hirak, and Bouteflika's long rule came to an end.
From painted rocks to peaceful marches, Algeria's people have kept shaping their own land.
